title: Flicker-DDPM: Accelerating Denoising Diffusion via 1/𝑓 Colored Noise Injection

paper.title: Flicker-DDPM: Accelerating Denoising Diffusion via 1 / f 1/f Colored Noise Injection
paper.abstract: Abstract We propose a novel diffusion model, Flicker-DDPM , which incorporates flicker ( 1 / f 1/f ) noise inspired by self-organized criticality (SOC), a widely observed phenomenon in natural systems. Unlike denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), which employ isotropic white noise in the forward process, Flicker-DDPM adopts colored noise with power-law spectra to better match the spectral statistics of natural images, whose power spectra typically follow P ⁡ ( k ) ∝ k − α P(k)\propto k^{-\alpha} . To this end, we develop a colored-noise module based on a spatial correlation kernel, σ ⁡ ( d ) = ( d + 1 ) − η \sigma(d)=(d+1)^{-\eta} , and theoretically establish that adjusting η \eta controls the spectral exponent α \alpha of the generated 1 / f α 1/f^{\alpha} noise, enabling adaptation to datasets with diverse spectral characteristics. On CIFAR-10, Flicker-DDPM matches or surpasses the generation quality of a standard DDPM baseline using 3.33 × 3.33\times fewer sampling steps, with negligible additional computational cost per step. We further develop a frequency-domain linear theory demonstrating that spectrally matched colored noise linearizes the reverse trajectory, theoretically explaining the observed sampling acceleration.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Flicker noise—random fluctuations whose power spectral density scales as S ⁡ ( f ) ∝ 1 / f α S(f)\propto 1/f^{\alpha} —is among the most ubiquitous phenomena in nature [ 29 ] . First identified in vacuum tubes in the 1920s, it has since been observed across an extraordinary range of systems: semiconductor devices [ 14 ] , X-ray luminosity variations from accreting black holes [ 44 ] , conformational dynamics of proteins [ 9 , 27 ] , long-range correlations in DNA sequences [ 31 ] , pitch and loudness fluctuations in music and speech [ 46 ] , and the statistics of natural images [ 36 , 43 , 35 , 45 , 38 ] . This universality is intimately connected to self-organized criticality (SOC) [ 4 , 5 ] , which posits that many complex systems naturally evolve toward critical states characterized by scale-free correlations and power-law relaxation spectra. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) [ 13 , 39 ] have achieved state-of-the-art generative performance in image synthesis [ 8 ] , molecular design [ 15 ] , audio generation [ 22 ] , and protein structure prediction [ 47 , 1 ] . The standard framework defines a forward process x t = α ¯ t ​ x 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ x_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,x_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) , progressively corrupting data into isotropic white Gaussian noise. A neural network then learns to reverse this process, generating samples from noise. A fundamental inefficiency arises from the spectral mismatch between white noise and structured data. Natural images have power spectra P data ​ ( k ) ∝ k − α P_{\text{data}}(k)\propto k^{-\alpha} with α ≈ 2 \alpha\approx 2 – 3 3 [ 43 ] , concentrating energy at low spatial frequencies. Similar power-law statistics appear in protein distance maps, audio spectrograms, and astrophysical time series. White noise, with its flat spectrum, forces the reverse process to simultaneously reshape the spectral profile and generate fine-grained structure—two tasks operating on incompatible time scales. This difficulty is compounded by the spectral bias of neural networks [ 32 ] , which preferentially learn low-frequency functions, potentially further degrading high-frequency generation quality. This issue is closely related to the noise schedule flaw identified by Lin et al. [ 24 ] , where non-zero terminal SNR causes residual low-frequency leakage during training but absence during inference—a problem also analyzed from the variational perspective [ 21 ] . Recent Fourier-space analysis [ 10 ] has independently confirmed that this frequency hierarchy—where high-frequency components are corrupted faster and suffer larger approximation errors—degrades generation quality. Frequency-aware noise control [ 18 ] , spectral regularization [ 7 ] , and non-isotropic forward processes such as inverse heat dissipation [ 33 ] have been proposed as partial remedies, though none provides an analytic prescription linking noise structure to data statistics. In this paper, we show that the multi-scale relaxation dynamics within trained DDPM—where the score-function response spans three orders of magnitude across frequencies—mirrors the broad relaxation spectra characteristic of SOC systems. Rather than treat this as an inherent property, we identify it as a consequence of the spectral mismatch and propose a direct solution: inject 1 / f 1/f -type colored noise whose spectrum matches the data. We construct a colored noise module with a single tunable parameter η \eta whose optimal value is analytically determined from data statistics via Matérn covariance theory, and integrate it into DDPM to create Flicker-DDPM . The result is a 3.33 × 3.33\times sampling speedup with quality improvement, at negligible computational overhead.

sections.heading: II Method
sections.text: Our approach proceeds in three steps: (i) we establish the general relationship between power-law spatial correlations and power-law spectra, showing that the desired 1 / f α 1/f^{\alpha} noise can be generated from a simple correlation kernel; (ii) we derive the kernel parameter η \eta analytically from the data spectrum via Matérn covariance theory; and (iii) we integrate the resulting colored noise into the DDPM forward and reverse processes with no architectural changes.

sections.heading: II.1 Power-law spectra from power-law correlations
sections.text: The connection between spatial correlations and spectral structure relies on a key statistical property of natural images: approximate translational and rotational invariance. Ensemble-averaged over natural scenes, the two-point correlation function depends only on the separation distance r = | 𝐫 1 − 𝐫 2 | r=|\mathbf{r}_{1}-\mathbf{r}_{2}| , not on absolute position or orientation [ 36 ] . For such statistically homogeneous and isotropic fields, the Wiener–Khinchin theorem reduces to a radial Hankel transform: S ⁡ ( k ) = 2 ​ π ​ ∫ 0 ∞ C ⁡ ( r ) ​ J 0 ​ ( k ​ r ) ​ r ​ 𝑑 r . S(k)=2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}C(r)\,J_{0}(kr)\,r\,dr. (1) Now suppose the correlation is a power law, C ⁡ ( r ) ∝ r − η C(r)\propto r^{-\eta} . Under rescaling r → λ ​ r r\to\lambda r , this function transforms homogeneously: C ⁡ ( λ ​ r ) = λ − η ​ C ​ ( r ) C(\lambda r)=\lambda^{-\eta}C(r) . The Hankel transform maps homogeneous functions to homogeneous functions—the integration measure r ​ d ​ r r\,dr contributes dimension 2, and the oscillatory kernel J 0 ​ ( k ​ r ) J_{0}(kr) enforces k → k / λ k\to k/\lambda —so the spectrum is necessarily a power law S ⁡ ( k ) ∝ k − α S(k)\propto k^{-\alpha} , with α \alpha determined by η \eta and the spatial dimension d = 2 d=2 . Power-law correlations produce power-law spectra, and vice versa. This duality motivates our approach: to generate noise with the 1 / f α 1/f^{\alpha} spectrum observed in natural images, it suffices to impose a power-law spatial correlation kernel. The spectrum inherits the power-law form automatically from the symmetry. The precise quantitative mapping η ⁡ ( α ) \eta(\alpha) —accounting for the finite correlation range of real data—is derived in Sec. II C via Matérn covariance theory.

sections.heading: III.2 Analysis of results
sections.text: Several features of Table 2 merit discussion: Robustness to step reduction. —The key observation is not merely that Flicker-DDPM is better at a fixed T T , but that its quality degrades far more gracefully as T T decreases. From T = 500 T=500 to T = 150 T=150 , white DDPM’s FID nearly doubles ( 13.02 → 25.36 13.02\to 25.36 ), whereas Flicker-DDPM’s FID increases by only 2 % 2\% ( 11.96 → 12.24 11.96\to 12.24 ). This insensitivity to T T is a direct consequence of the spectral matching condition L ⁡ ( 𝐤 ) = 0 L(\mathbf{k})=0 : when the noise already carries the correct frequency structure, the reverse process need not spend steps reshaping the spectrum, and shorter trajectories suffice. Diminishing gap at large T T . —At T = 500 T=500 , the FID difference narrows to 8 % 8\% . This is expected: given enough steps, even white DDPM eventually completes the spectral restructuring—the nonlinear dynamics just take longer. The colored-noise advantage is precisely that it eliminates this bottleneck. Training convergence. —Figure 4 shows that Flicker-DDPM at T = 150 T=150 converges to a lower FID asymptote than white DDPM at T = 500 T=500 , and does so in fewer training epochs. The training objective itself is easier to minimize when the noise matches data statistics: at each timestep, the denoising target ϵ \epsilon has spatial correlations consistent with the signal to be recovered, reducing the effective complexity of the learning problem. Architectural universality. —Flicker-DDPM requires no architectural modifications. The same UNet trained with white noise can be retrained with colored noise by changing only the noise generation module. This makes the approach a drop-in replacement applicable to any existing DDPM pipeline.

sections.heading: IV Theoretical Explanation
sections.text: The central theoretical insight is that colored noise linearizes the reverse diffusion dynamics in Fourier space. We develop a frequency-domain linear theory that quantitatively predicts the spectral evolution of the reverse process and explains why Flicker-DDPM requires far fewer steps than white-noise DDPM. In the Supplemental Material, we further reformulate the stochastic dynamics using the MSRJD path integral [ 26 , 17 ] , which provides a systematic perturbation theory for nonlinear mode-coupling corrections (Appendix E and F ).

sections.heading: IV.1 Frequency-domain linearization

A pixel-space linear approximation s θ ​ ( x ) ≈ A ​ x + b s_{\theta}(x)\approx Ax+b would be crude and inaccurate—trained denoisers are highly nonlinear functions of x x . Our approach instead works in the spatial Fourier basis : for translationally invariant data, the score function’s Jacobian ∂ s θ / ∂ x \partial s_{\theta}/\partial x is a circulant matrix (to leading order), which is diagonal in Fourier space. sections.heading: V Discussion and Outlook
sections.text: Flicker-DDPM demonstrates that matching noise statistics to data statistics yields substantial practical gains through a simple, principled modification. The underlying physics is clear: SOC-like multi-scale dynamics in standard DDPM are not intrinsic but arise from spectral mismatch, and are eliminated when the noise carries the correct 1 / f 1/f structure. The universality of Eq. ( 4 ) suggests broad applicability. Power-law spectra characterize not only natural images but also protein distance correlations [ 9 , 27 ] , astrophysical variability [ 44 ] , audio signals [ 46 ] , and electronic noise [ 14 ] . We note that Eq. ( 4 ) is derived specifically for d = 2 d=2 spatial dimensions and the Matérn covariance family; for data of other dimensionality or different correlation structures, the same spectral-matching methodology applies—measure the data power spectrum, identify an appropriate covariance model, and match the noise kernel parameters accordingly—but the specific formula relating α \alpha to η \eta will differ. The approach is orthogonal to existing acceleration methods (DDIM [ 40 ] , progressive distillation [ 37 ] , consistency models [ 41 ] ) and complementary to noise-schedule design principles [ 19 ] ; it may be combined with them for further gains. One limitation of the pure power-law noise model is its imprecision at high spatial frequencies: real image spectra deviate from a strict k − α k^{-\alpha} law in the high- k k regime, and the power-law kernel systematically underweights fine-scale texture. A promising extension is to augment high-frequency noise strength beyond the 1 / f α 1/f^{\alpha} envelope—for instance, incorporating blue-noise correlations that preferentially enhance high-frequency content [ 16 ] . Combining the low-frequency fidelity of Flicker-DDPM with targeted high-frequency boosting may further improve texture sharpness without sacrificing the acceleration benefits demonstrated here. Keywords: diffusion models, 1 / f 1/f noise, self-organized criticality, colored noise, generative models I Introduction Flicker noise—random fluctuations whose power spectral density scales as S ⁡ ( f ) ∝ 1 / f α S(f)\propto 1/f^{\alpha} —is among the most ubiquitous phenomena in nature [ 29 ] . First identified in vacuum tubes in the 1920s, it has since been observed across an extraordinary range of systems: semiconductor devices [ 14 ] , X-ray luminosity variations from accreting black holes [ 44 ] , conformational dynamics of proteins [ 9 , 27 ] , long-range correlations in DNA sequences [ 31 ] , pitch and loudness fluctuations in music and speech [ 46 ] , and the statistics of natural images [ 36 , 43 , 35 , 45 , 38 ] . This universality is intimately connected to self-organized criticality (SOC) [ 4 , 5 ] , which posits that many complex systems naturally evolve toward critical states characterized by scale-free correlations and power-law relaxation spectra. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) [ 13 , 39 ] have achieved state-of-the-art generative performance in image synthesis [ 8 ] , molecular design [ 15 ] , audio generation [ 22 ] , and protein structure prediction [ 47 , 1 ] . The standard framework defines a forward process x t = α ¯ t ​ x 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ x_{t}=\sqrt{ ar{\alpha}_{t}}\,x_{0}+\sqrt{1- ar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) , progressively corrupting data into isotropic white Gaussian noise. A neural network then learns to reverse this process, generating samples from noise. A fundamental inefficiency arises from the spectral mismatch between white noise and structured data. Natural images have power spectra P data ​ ( k ) ∝ k − α P_{	ext{data}}(k)\propto k^{-\alpha} with α ≈ 2 \alpha\approx 2 – 3 3 [ 43 ] , concentrating energy at low spatial frequencies. Similar power-law statistics appear in protein distance maps, audio spectrograms, and astrophysical time series. White noise, with its flat spectrum, forces the reverse process to simultaneously reshape the spectral profile and generate fine-grained structure—two tasks operating on incompatible time scales. This difficulty is compounded by the spectral bias of neural networks [ 32 ] , which preferentially learn low-frequency functions, potentially further degrading high-frequency generation quality. This issue is closely related to the noise schedule flaw identified by Lin et al. [ 24 ] , where non-zero terminal SNR causes residual low-frequency leakage during training but absence during inference—a problem also analyzed from the variational perspective [ 21 ] . Recent Fourier-space analysis [ 10 ] has independently confirmed that this frequency hierarchy—where high-frequency components are corrupted faster and suffer larger approximation errors—degrades generation quality. Frequency-aware noise control [ 18 ] , spectral regularization [ 7 ] , and non-isotropic forward processes such as inverse heat dissipation [ 33 ] have been proposed as partial remedies, though none provides an analytic prescription linking noise structure to data statistics. In this paper, we show that the multi-scale relaxation dynamics within trained DDPM—where the score-function response spans three orders of magnitude across frequencies—mirrors the broad relaxation spectra characteristic of SOC systems. Rather than treat this as an inherent property, we identify it as a consequence of the spectral mismatch and propose a direct solution: inject 1 / f 1/f -type colored noise whose spectrum matches the data. We construct a colored noise module with a single tunable parameter η \eta whose optimal value is analytically determined from data statistics via Matérn covariance theory, and integrate it into DDPM to create Flicker-DDPM . The result is a 3.33 × 3.33	imes sampling speedup with quality improvement, at negligible computational overhead. II Method Our approach proceeds in three steps: (i) we establish the general relationship between power-law spatial correlations and power-law spectra, showing that the desired 1 / f α 1/f^{\alpha} noise can be generated from a simple correlation kernel; (ii) we derive the kernel parameter η \eta analytically from the data spectrum via Matérn covariance theory; and (iii) we integrate the resulting colored noise into the DDPM forward and reverse processes with no architectural changes. V Discussion and Outlook Flicker-DDPM demonstrates that matching noise statistics to data statistics yields substantial practical gains through a simple, principled modification. The underlying physics is clear: SOC-like multi-scale dynamics in standard DDPM are not intrinsic but arise from spectral mismatch, and are eliminated when the noise carries the correct 1 / f 1/f structure. The universality of Eq. ( 4 ) suggests broad applicability. Power-law spectra characterize not only natural images but also protein distance correlations [ 9 , 27 ] , astrophysical variability [ 44 ] , audio signals [ 46 ] , and electronic noise [ 14 ] . We note that Eq. ( 4 ) is derived specifically for d = 2 d=2 spatial dimensions and the Matérn covariance family; for data of other dimensionality or different correlation structures, the same spectral-matching methodology applies—measure the data power spectrum, identify an appropriate covariance model, and match the noise kernel parameters accordingly—but the specific formula relating α \alpha to η \eta will differ. The approach is orthogonal to existing acceleration methods (DDIM [ 40 ] , progressive distillation [ 37 ] , consistency models [ 41 ] ) and complementary to noise-schedule design principles [ 19 ] ; it may be combined with them for further gains. One limitation of the pure power-law noise model is its imprecision at high spatial frequencies: real image spectra deviate from a strict k − α k^{-\alpha} law in the high- k k regime, and the power-law kernel systematically underweights fine-scale texture. A promising extension is to augment high-frequency noise strength beyond the 1 / f α 1/f^{\alpha} envelope—for instance, incorporating blue-noise correlations that preferentially enhance high-frequency content [ 16 ] . Combining the low-frequency fidelity of Flicker-DDPM with targeted high-frequency boosting may further improve texture sharpness without sacrificing the acceleration benefits demonstrated here.
